contributions.headingText: MALT lymphoma of the dura is a distinctive low-grade lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) composed of marginal zone B cells, sometimes with plasmacytic differentiation, arising in the dura.
2A85.3 Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, primary site excluding stomach or skin
Acceptable: extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

Lymphomas arising in the dura mater are much less frequent than those arising in the brain {16769960}. By far the most common dural lymphoma is MALT lymphoma {8990144; 11838814}. MALT lymphoma originating in the dura is much more common than MALT lymphoma originating in the brain {29103980; 31808316}. Most MALT lymphomas arise in the cranial dura; a small minority arise in the dura covering the spinal cord {21102421; 32318699}, and these may be associated with spinal cord compression {21785250}.
Patients may present with headache, seizures, visual changes, focal neurological defects, and other symptoms {8990144; 9832258; 10965827; 16769960; 21785250; 21102421; 27248180; 29103980}.

Dural MALT lymphoma affects adults, with a median age in the sixth decade {29103980; 31808316}. Women are affected more often than men, with an M:F ratio of approximately 1:5–7 {16009945; 16769960; 21102421; 27248180}. No racial or geographical associations have been identified.

MALT lymphoma outside the CNS has been attributed to chronic inflammation (of either infectious or autoimmune origin) {24333758}. Regarding MALT lymphoma of the dura, it is still unknown whether there is an association with inflammatory disorders. One patient with hepatitis C who developed dural MALT lymphoma has been reported {32494320}. One patient with CNS extranodal marginal zone lymphoma had a long history of white matter disease with some features of multiple sclerosis {22520340}, and another patient with extranodal marginal zone lymphoma had Chlamydia psittaci infection {21239044}.

Trisomies, most often of chromosome 3, are occasionally detected {16009945; 21102421}. Inactivation of TNFAIP3 by mutation or loss appears common in cases with plasmacytic differentiation {27248180}. Activating NOTCH2 mutations accompanied by inactivating TBL1XR1 mutations are common in cases with monocytoid morphology {27248180}. Recurrent gains of 6p25.3 and losses at 1p36.32 have been documented. IGH translocation and MALT lymphoma–associated translocations are rare {29103980; 32318699}, but a translocation involving the MALT1 and IGH genes, consistent with IGH::MALT1 fusion [t(14;18)(q32;q21)], has been identified in 1 case {19669212}.
There is a solitary mass or plaque-like thickening of the dura {8990144; 16009945; 16769960; 21785250; 21102421}, often mimicking a meningioma {29103980}.

Dural MALT lymphomas share histological and immunohistological features with MALT lymphomas at other sites. They are composed of small lymphocytes and marginal zone cells, often with plasmacytic differentiation, sometimes with remnants of reactive follicles with follicular colonization {8990144; 9832258; 16009945; 16769960; 21102421}. A subset of cases have tumour cells with abundant clear cytoplasm (monocytoid morphology) {27248180}. Occasionally, associated amyloid deposition is seen {11838814; 16009945}. Dural MALT lymphomas may arise in association with meningothelium (just as marginal zone lymphomas often arise in association with epithelium in other sites), so entrapped meningothelial cells may be present {8990144; 11838814}. Infrequently, lymphoma cells invade Virchow–Robin spaces and the subjacent brain parenchyma {21102421}.

Immunohistochemistry

Neoplastic B cells are CD20+, CD79a+, CD5−, CD10−, BCL6−, CD23−, IRF4 (MUM1)+/−, cyclin D1−, BCL2+, and they have a low proliferation index {27248180; 29103980; 32318699}. A component of clonal plasma cells is often found {21785250; 21102421}. The monotypic plasma cells are often IgG4+ {21102421; 27248180}, but evidence of systemic IgG4-related disease has been absent to date {21102421}.
MALT lymphomas of the dura are typically localized at presentation {8990144; 16009945; 16769960; 21102421}. Clinical staging is performed to exclude extracranial manifestations.

Patients are treated with resection, radiation, and/or chemotherapy, and they typically achieve complete remission {26194368; 27248180; 29103980; 32318699; 31808316}. The prognosis is very good. One case series reported 22 complete remissions and 1 partial response in 23 evaluable patients, with a 3-year progression-free survival rate of 89% {27649904}. Local and systemic relapses are rare {16769960; 27649904}.
